theory.intro: The **shape** of a distribution is described by its **modality** and **skewness**. Modality counts the peaks. Skewness describes how symmetrical the distribution is. Skew is named from the **tail** — the side where the frequencies taper off and stretch away from the bulk of the data.
facts: To name the skew, find where most of the data sits, then compare how the frequencies trail off on each side. Also check how many separated peaks the display has.
Name the skew by the **tail**, never by the peak.

For a single-peaked distribution, tall columns near the left followed by frequencies tapering off over a longer stretch to the right indicate positive skew. Tall columns on the left alone do not establish positive skew; a display with several peaks needs its whole shape considered.

The distribution is **symmetrical**.

Curve $C$ has a longer tail to the left, so **curve $C$ is negatively skewed**.

workedExamples.question_text:
Describe the shape of the distribution of retirement ages.

| Retirement age (years) | Frequency |
| --- | --- |
| 35–39 | 1 |
| 40–44 | 2 |
| 45–49 | 4 |
| 50–54 | 8 |
| 55–59 | 15 |
| 60–64 | 24 |
| 65–69 | 12 |
workedExamples.solution_text:
The largest frequency is $24$, in the $60$–$64$ age group. The frequencies taper off through $15,8,4,2,1$ across five groups to the left, with only one group to the right.

The tail stretches to the left, so the distribution is **negatively skewed**.

**a.** There are two separated peaks, at $25$ and $55$, with a dip between them. The heights $2,10,4,4,10,2$ read the same forwards and backwards, so the whole display has mirrored halves.

The distribution is **bimodal and symmetrical**.

**b.** Every column has frequency $6$, so there is no distinct peak. The two halves are mirror images.

The distribution is **uniform and symmetrical**.

Each curve shows a possible distribution of test marks, with marks increasing from left to right.
A very difficult test was sat by $180$ students. Most scored low marks and only a few scored high marks.
Which curve, $A$, $B$ or $C$, is most likely to show their marks?
foundation.solution_text:
Most students scored low marks, so the bulk of the data sits on the left and the few high marks trail away to the right.
Curve $B$ shows this positively skewed distribution.

foundation.question_text:
The frequency table shows the marks of $52$ students on an exam.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{Mark} & \text{Frequency} \\ \hline 0\text{--}19 & 2 \\ \hline 20\text{--}39 & 5 \\ \hline 40\text{--}59 & 11 \\ \hline 60\text{--}79 & 20 \\ \hline 80\text{--}100 & 14 \\ \hline \end{array}$
Describe the shape of this distribution.
foundation.solution_text:
The largest frequency is $20$, at $60\text{--}79$, so most of the data sits on the right.
The frequencies fall away over the classes $40\text{--}59$, $20\text{--}39$ and $0\text{--}19$ on the left.
The tail stretches to the left, so the distribution is negatively skewed.
